nameStory: The Beechwood Woodwart gets its name from its strong preference for growing on dead beech wood, where it forms dark, warty bumps that look like woody growths sprouting from the bark. The "woodwart" part perfectly captures its appearance - these fungi create irregular, bumpy patches that really do resemble warts on the tree's surface. It's named after mycologist Jack Rogers, who made significant contributions to studying these wood-dwelling fungi.
description: Beechwood Woodwart is a hard, crusty fungus that grows directly on dead beech wood, forming dark patches that look like charcoal-colored bumps or blisters. These fungi are saprophytes, meaning they help decompose dead wood by breaking it down into nutrients for the forest. The fruiting bodies appear as irregular, warty masses that can be anywhere from penny-sized to covering several inches of bark. They're part of the "carbon fungus" group, known for their distinctive black, crusty appearance.

idTips.label: Host specificity
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on dead beech trees and branches - if you're not looking at beech wood, it's probably not this species

idTips.label: Texture and hardness
idTips.description: Feels extremely hard and crusty when dry, like touching charcoal or burnt wood, but may soften slightly when wet

idTips.label: Color and appearance
idTips.description: Deep black to dark grayish-black surface that looks almost burnt, with an irregular warty or blistered texture

idTips.label: Growth pattern
idTips.description: Forms scattered bumpy patches rather than continuous crusts, often clustered together on the same piece of wood

idTips.label: Interior color
idTips.description: If broken open, reveals a white to cream-colored interior that contrasts sharply with the black exterior

habitat: Found in mature hardwood forests throughout New England, particularly in areas with abundant American beech trees. Look for it on fallen beech logs, dead standing beech trees, and large dead branches in mixed deciduous forests at elevations from sea level to about 2,000 feet. It thrives in moist woodland environments where dead beech wood can slowly decompose over several years.

seasonality.spring: Existing fruiting bodies become more noticeable as they absorb moisture and may darken further. New growth may begin on recently fallen beech wood.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when new fruiting bodies develop and mature. The black crusty surfaces are most prominent and easy to spot against lighter-colored beech bark.
seasonality.fall: Mature fruiting bodies are well-developed and highly visible. This is often the best time for identification as the contrast with fallen autumn leaves makes them stand out.
seasonality.winter: Fruiting bodies persist and remain identifiable under snow, though they may appear somewhat weathered. The hard, crusty texture helps them survive freezing temperatures.

funFact: Beechwood Woodwart can actually help forensic investigators determine how long a beech tree has been dead - these fungi have predictable colonization patterns that act like a natural timeline, with different species appearing in sequence as the wood decomposes over months and years.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other dark crusty fungi on hardwood, but the exclusive relationship with beech wood is the key distinguisher - if it's growing on oak, maple, or any other tree species, it's definitely something else. Remember: "Beech-wood Woodwart belongs on beech" for the alliteration.
contextualKnowledge: The genus Jackrogersella was recently separated from the genus Hypoxylon based on DNA studies, so older field guides may list this species under its former name. This represents how modern genetic analysis is reshaping our understanding of fungal relationships, even for species that look quite similar to the naked eye.
compareHints: Beechwood Woodwart differs from its relative Birch Woodwart primarily by its host preference - Birch Woodwart grows on birch trees and tends to form more continuous crusty patches rather than the discrete warty bumps typical of the beech species. The Birch Woodwart also tends to have a slightly more grayish tone compared to the deep black color of fresh Beechwood Woodwart. When in doubt, check what type of tree you're looking at first.
